title: Percentage Increase, Decrease and Absolute Change
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Number
summary: Increase and decrease amounts by a percentage with and without a calculator, use multipliers, and find and compare absolute and percentage changes.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand percentage increase and percentage decrease, and absolute change — increase or decrease an amount by a percentage, and find the change as an amount and as a percentage of the original (8Nf.05)

blocks.text: Prices go up, sales take money off, populations grow, a phone battery runs down. There are two ways to describe any change: the **absolute change** (the actual amount it went up or down by, in dollars, kilograms, people…) and the **percentage change** (how big the change is compared with the original amount). This page teaches both, and shows why they can tell different stories.
Key words

items: percentage (%)
نسبة مئوية — a number out of 100: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15
original amount
القيمة الأصلية — the amount before the change; percentages of change are always of this amount
increase
زيادة — go up
decrease
نقص / تخفيض — go down
absolute change
التغير المطلق — the actual amount of the change: new amount − original amount
percentage change
التغير بالنسبة المئوية — the change as a percentage of the original: change ÷ original × 100
multiplier
المضروب فيه (المعامل) — the single number you multiply by: increase by 15% → × 1.15
discount
خصم — a decrease in price, often given as a percentage

blocks.text: 1. Absolute change and percentage change
**Absolute change = new amount − original amount.** It has the same units as the amounts. A positive answer is an increase; a negative answer is a decrease.
**Percentage change = (change ÷ original amount) × 100.** It compares the change with where you **started**.

blocks.text: So "Which price rose more?" has two possible answers. Shop B had the bigger **absolute** increase; Shop A had the bigger **percentage** increase. In a Checkpoint question, always say which one you mean, and back it up with numbers.
2. Increasing an amount by a percentage
**Method 1 — find the percentage, then add it on.** This is best without a calculator. Build the percentage from easy parts: 10% (÷ 10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷ 100), 50% (÷ 2), 25% (÷ 4).

blocks.text: **Method 2 — use a multiplier.** The new amount is 100% + 15% = 115% of the original, and 115% = 1.15. So multiply by **1.15**: $60 × 1.15 = $69. This is one step on a calculator.
3. Decreasing an amount by a percentage
**Method 1:** find the percentage and **subtract** it. **Method 2:** the new amount is 100% − 20% = 80% of the original, so multiply by **0.8**.

blocks.text: **Quick check:** an increase multiplier is **more than 1**; a decrease multiplier is **less than 1**. An increase of 7% is × 1.07, not × 1.7 (that would be a 70% increase).

blocks.title: افتكر القاعدة دي
items: التغير المطلق = الجديد − الأصلي (بالجنيه أو الكيلو…).
النسبة المئوية للتغير = (التغير ÷ الأصلي) × ١٠٠ — دايماً اقسم على القيمة الأصلية، مش الجديدة.
زيادة ١٥٪ يعني اضرب في ١٫١٥، ونقص ٢٠٪ يعني اضرب في ٠٫٨.

blocks.text: 4. Finding the percentage change

items: Find the absolute change: new − original.
Divide by the **original** amount.
Multiply by 100 and write %. Say whether it is an increase or a decrease.

blocks.text: **Without a calculator** write the change as a fraction of the original and make the denominator 100: 12/80 = 3/20 = 15/100 = 15%. And 35/250 = 7/50 = 14/100 = 14%.
5. One change after another
A price of $500 goes up by 10%, then the new price goes down by 10%. Is it back to $500?

items: It is **not** back to $500, because the second 10% is a percentage of $550, not of $500. Overall: absolute change −$5, percentage change 5 ÷ 500 × 100 = 1% decrease.

blocks.text: This is a favourite "Is he correct? Explain" question. Always ask: **a percentage of which amount?**
Worked examples
**Worked example 1 (no calculator)** — A gym membership costs $240 a year. The price increases by 15%. Work out the new price. [2 marks]
**Common mistake:** giving $36 as the final answer. The question asks for the new price, so add the increase on.
**Worked example 2 (calculator)** — A car is worth $8400. Its value decreases by 35%. Work out its new value. [2 marks]
**Worked example 3** — The number of students in a school went from 2400 to 2760. (a) Work out the absolute change. (b) Work out the percentage change. [3 marks]

items: (a) 2760 − 2400 = **360 students** (an increase).

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** dividing by the new number (360 ÷ 2760 = 13.0…%). The percentage change always uses the original.
**Worked example 4** — Hoda's bag of flour had a mass of 1.6 kg. After baking it had a mass of 1.2 kg. Work out the percentage decrease in the mass. [2 marks]
**Worked example 5** — Two shops sell the same phone. Shop P: was $300, now 20% off. Shop Q: was $280, now $50 off. Which shop is cheaper now? Show your working. [2 marks]

items: **Shop Q is cheaper** (by $10). Notice: Shop P's discount is $60 (bigger absolute discount), but the starting prices were different, so you must compare the final prices.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Youssef says, "If a price goes up by 10% and then down by 10%, it ends up the same." Use a price of $500 to show that Youssef is wrong. [2 marks]

$500 × 1.1 = $550 (1 mark). $550 × 0.9 = $495, which is not $500, so Youssef is **wrong**. The 10% decrease is taken from the bigger amount, $550, so it removes more ($55) than the increase added ($50).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Giving only the increase (e.g. $36) when the question asks for the new amount.
Using the wrong multiplier: increase by 7% is × 1.07, not × 1.7 or × 0.07; decrease by 35% is × 0.65, not × 0.35.
Dividing by the new amount instead of the original when finding a percentage change.
Mixing up absolute and percentage change — the absolute change has units ($, kg, people); the percentage change has %.
Thinking that +10% then −10% gets you back to the start.
Forgetting to say whether the change is an increase or a decrease.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Non-calculator paper: "Increase 80 by 15%" — build the percentage from 10%, 5% and 1%, and show those steps for method marks.
Calculator paper: real-life contexts (prices, populations, masses) — use a multiplier and write the calculation, e.g. 8400 × 0.65.
Two-part questions: "(a) Work out the absolute change (b) Work out the percentage change." Give units in (a) and % in (b).
"Which is the better deal?" or "Which had the greater increase?" — calculate both, then write a clear sentence comparing them.
"Is he correct? Explain your answer." — use a numerical example as your evidence (Thinking and Working Mathematically: convincing).
"Draw a ring around" the correct multiplier or the correct new amount.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Percentage change — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. Questions 1–6 without a calculator; a calculator may be used where it says so. Type numbers only (no $ or % sign needed). For the explain questions, mark yourself with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Draw a ring around the multiplier for an increase of 7%.
questions.e: 100% + 7% = 107% = 1.07. (1.7 would be a 70% increase; 0.93 is a 7% decrease; 0.07 only finds the 7%.)

questions.q: Draw a ring around the multiplier for a decrease of 35%.
questions.e: 100% − 35% = 65% = 0.65. Multiplying by 0.35 would give only the amount taken off.

questions.p: The price of a bag goes up from $40 to $46.
questions.q: (a) Work out the absolute change in the price.

questions.p: The price of a bag goes up from $40 to $46.

questions.q: A calculator may be used. Increase $360 by 12.5%.
A calculator may be used. A laptop costs $1250. In a sale the price is reduced by 18%. Work out the sale price.
The mass of a melon goes down from 2.5 kg to 2.1 kg as it dries. Work out the percentage decrease in its mass.
Town A grows from 5000 to 5500 people. Town B grows from 800 to 960 people. Which statement is true?
c: Town A has the greater absolute increase and the greater percentage increase.
Town B has the greater absolute increase and the greater percentage increase.
Both towns have the same percentage increase.
Town A has the greater absolute increase, but Town B has the greater percentage increase.
questions.e: Town A: +500 people, 500 ÷ 5000 × 100 = 10%. Town B: +160 people, 160 ÷ 800 × 100 = 20%. A has the bigger absolute increase; B has the bigger percentage increase.

questions.p: A shirt costs $50. Its price is increased by 20%. Later the new price is decreased by 20%.
questions.q: (a) Work out the final price of the shirt.
questions.e: 50 × 1.2 = $60 (1 mark). 60 × 0.8 = $48. The 20% decrease is 20% of $60 = $12, which is more than the $10 that was added.

questions.p: A shirt costs $50. Its price is increased by 20%. Later the new price is decreased by 20%.
questions.q: (b) Work out the overall percentage decrease from the original price of $50.
Ali says, "A rise from 3 to 6 is a 200% increase, because 6 is double 3." Is Ali correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Not correct, with a reason, e.g. the increase is 3, and 3 ÷ 3 × 100 = 100%; or 6 is 200% OF 3, but the increase is 100%; or doubling is a 100% increase. Do not accept "No" without a reason.
questions.e: Not correct. The absolute change is 6 − 3 = 3. Percentage increase = 3 ÷ 3 × 100 = 100%. The new value 6 is 200% of the original, but the increase is only 100%. A 200% increase would give 3 + 6 = 9.

questions.q: A calculator may be used. Shop X sells a jacket for $120 with 25% off. Shop Y sells the same jacket for $110 with 15% off. Which shop is cheaper? Show your working.
questions.ms: 1 mark: one correct sale price, $90 (Shop X) or $93.50 (Shop Y). 1 mark: both correct and the conclusion Shop X is cheaper (accept 'by $3.50'). Do not award the second mark for 'Shop X' with no working.
questions.e: Shop X: 120 × 0.75 = $90. Shop Y: 110 × 0.85 = $93.50. Shop X is cheaper, by $3.50 — even though its original price was higher.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Absolute change = new − original (with units). Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 (with %).
Always compare with the ORIGINAL amount.
Increase by r%: multiply by (100 + r)/100, e.g. 15% → × 1.15. Decrease by r%: multiply by (100 − r)/100, e.g. 20% → × 0.8.
No calculator: build percentages from 10%, 5% and 1%.
A bigger absolute change is not always a bigger percentage change — and +10% then −10% does not return to the start.
